body.objective: Students will be able to apply the sociological imagination.
body.iCan: I can apply the sociological imagination.
successCriteria: I can explain the sociological imagination
I can connect a personal experience to larger social forces
I can tell the difference between a personal trouble and a public issue
body.hook: You might think your choices are entirely your own: what you wear, what you eat, what job you want. Sociologist C. Wright Mills argued that personal lives are shaped by larger social forces like the economy, culture and history. He called seeing these connections the "sociological imagination."

vocabulary.definition: The study of society, social groups and how they shape human behaviour.
The ability to see how personal experiences connect to larger social forces.
A problem experienced by an individual.
A problem affecting many people that comes from social structures.
Patterns in society, such as the economy, education and family systems.
An influence from society, such as culture, technology or the economy.

study.title: Personal Troubles, Public Issues
study.question: How do social forces shape our lives?
study.passage:
C. Wright Mills (1959) distinguished:
• Personal trouble: one person can't find a job.
• Public issue: when thousands of people can't find jobs, the cause lies in the economy, not just in individuals.
Cases:
A. Maya, 17, works 20 hours a week at a fast-food restaurant and is falling behind in school.
B. Liam spends 6 hours a day on social media and feels anxious when he compares himself to others.
C. Priya's family moved from a rural Alberta town to Calgary because her parents' jobs ended when a local plant closed.
D. Ethan can't afford to move out after graduating because rent in his city has risen sharply.
For each case, ask:
1. What is the personal trouble?
2. What larger social forces might be involved (economy, technology, culture, government policy)?
3. Is this happening to many people? How could you find out (for example, Statistics Canada data)?
4. What would an individual solution be, and what would a social solution be?
Personal connection: Write about one choice in your own life (your phone, your clothes, your plans after high school) and identify two social forces that influence it.
study.source: Original cases written for this lesson; concept from C. Wright Mills, The Sociological Imagination (1959).
steps: Distinguish personal troubles and public issues
Apply the idea to your own life
discussion: Which case shows the clearest public issue? Why?
What social forces affect Liam's anxiety?
Why might an individual solution not be enough for Ethan?
How did your own choice connect to social forces?
study.product: Write a short essay applying the sociological imagination to one case or your own life: describe the personal trouble, identify at least two social forces, and compare an individual and a social solution.

examples.title: Personal vs public
examples.problem: One student fails a test. Personal trouble or public issue?
examples.explore: When would failing grades become a public issue?

examples.title: Social forces
examples.problem: What social forces affect Priya's family?
examples.answer: The plant closure and economic change in rural Alberta
examples.explore: How many families might be affected?

examples.title: Solutions
examples.problem: What social solution could help Ethan?
examples.answer: More affordable housing or rental policies
examples.explore: Why might an individual solution be limited?

examples.title: Using data
examples.problem: How could you check whether Maya's situation is common?
examples.answer: Statistics Canada data on students working part-time
examples.explore: Why is data important in sociology?

practice.q: Give an example of a social force.
practice.a: The economy (also culture, technology, government policy).

practice.q: What is the personal trouble in Case D?
practice.a: Ethan can't afford to move out.

practice.q: Where could you find data on Canadian trends?
What year did Mills publish his idea?

practice.a: Patterns in society such as the economy and education systems.

practice.q: Why isn't unemployment only a personal trouble?
practice.a: When many people are affected, the cause lies in the economy.

practice.q: How can technology be a social force in Liam's case?
practice.a: Social media design and culture shape his habits and comparisons.

practice.q: Why might social solutions be needed alongside individual ones?
practice.a: Individual effort can't fix problems caused by larger structures.

practice.q: How does the sociological imagination change how we judge others?
practice.a: It shows that circumstances, not just choices, shape people's lives.

misconceptions: Thinking all problems are caused only by individual choices
Ignoring data when deciding if something is a public issue
Thinking social forces remove all personal responsibility
